newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Race for Slovenia power wide open, rightist says.
newsitem.headline: Race for Slovenia power wide open, rightist says.

text.p: Slovenia's rightist People's Party leader Marjan Podobnik said on Monday an alliance of right-wing parties would probably win enough parliamentary seats to form the next government.
"The "Spring' (rightwing alliance) will have between 44 and 46 seats in the (90-seat) parliament and I expect to become the next prime minister," Podobnik, 36, told Reuters.
Speaking a day after Slovenia's second general election since independence from Yugoslavia in 1991, Podobnik said the country should not rush into membership of the European Union and NATO.

The three-party rightwing alliance, called the "Slovenian Spring", may turn to representatives of the ethnic Hungarian and Italian communities, who are allocated a seat each in parliament, to tip the balance for a majority in parliament.
But Podobnik declined to rule out a possible coalition with Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek's centre-left Liberal Democrats if the rightist group failed to gain at least 46 seats in parliament.

Podobnik, speaking to Reuters by telephone, said he backed Slovenia's future membership of the European Union and the NATO military alliance, but argued that the process had to be given more consideration to protect Slovenian interests.
"We need clear protection in our legislation before we consider changing the constitution...and protect our vital national interests such as border areas and farming," he said.
Podobnik's People's Party, largely backed by farmers, won 19.59 percent in Sunday's election, according to unofficial results.

The other two parties in the "Spring", the centre-right Social Democrats and the conservative Christian Democrats, won 16.03 and 9.52 percent respectively. Final official results were expected by the end of the week.
Drnovsek, whose Liberal Democrats won most votes with 27.1 percent, was expected to be called first by President Milan Kucan to form a new coalition.
But the current premier will be forced to seek a partnership with one or two of the rightwing parties to have any chance of leading the next government.
The new administration will have to adopt a raft of tough economic reforms and spending cuts to enable Slovenia to maintain its position as one of the most prosperous of Europe's ex-communist states.
Slovenian political analyst Miha Kovac said a clear shift to the right, without the Liberal Democrats in government, could spell trouble for Slovenia.
He said a rightist government would slow down the already sluggish privatisation process and may want to revise privatisations which have taken place over the past four years.
"If they form a government, foreign investment will stay in the doldrums. The climate will be more favourable if Drnovsek stays in power," he added.
